---
title: "Jestyr"
---

Jestyr is a from-scratch systems language built to answer one question:
**how much of Rust-grade memory safety and C-grade performance survives
dropping lifetimes entirely?**

Its answer is a tiered reference model — second-class borrows that
provably cannot outlive their frame, generation-checked references that
turn use-after-free into a deterministic fault, and scope-bounded
`region` allocation — validated at real scale: the compiler is written
in Jestyr and compiles itself. Two independent implementations of the
same compiler — a ~52,000-line Rust reference and a 29,818-line
self-hosted Jestyr port — are held byte-identical in their C output over
a 148-file corpus, and a committed bootstrap seed builds the whole
toolchain with nothing but a C compiler.

This is a research release (`v0.1.0-research`), not a production tool.
See [Research](research.qmd) for what is and isn't claimed.

## Try it in two commands (no Rust required)

The repository commits the compiler's own C output for its own source.
Build it, then watch it regenerate that seed byte-for-byte:

```bash
gcc -O2 -std=c11 -ffp-contract=off -fno-fast-math -o jc bootstrap/jestyr_seed.c
```

```bash
./jc bootstrap/jestyr_flat.jtr > regen.c && diff regen.c bootstrap/jestyr_seed.c
```

::: {.program-output}
(empty diff)
:::

An empty diff is the self-hosting fixed point: the compiler you just
built from the seed reproduces the seed, byte for byte. Cold clone to
working compiler takes roughly 21–30 seconds on a laptop. From there,
`./jc examples/hello.jtr run` compiles and runs a program. On
Windows/MinGW add `-Wl,--stack,67108864` to the gcc line; details in
[Get started](get-started.qmd).

## The language, briefly

```{.rust}
fn sum(read xs: [3]i32) -> i32 {     // `read`: a borrow, provably
    var total: i32 = 0               //  frame-bounded — no lifetime
    for read x in xs {               //  annotations, ever
        total = total + x
    }
    return total
}

fn main() -> i32 {
    var xs: [3]i32 = [10, 20, 30]    // a stack VALUE that moves, copies,
    print_int(sum(xs))               // and drops by scope — RAII, no GC
    return 0
}
```

::: {.program-output}
60
:::

Values are owned and moved. Borrows (`read`/`mut`) are second-class —
they can be passed down but never stored or returned, so the escape
checker's guarantee is structural, not inferred. Data structures that
need stored references get generation-checked `genref`s or `region`
arenas whose escapes are compile errors. Errors are checked sets with
stack-only payloads. Cost models are attributes the compiler enforces:
serializing a `par for` under `@span` is a compile error, `@simd` is a
checked legality claim, `@deterministic` rejects non-deterministic
reductions. The full walk-through is in the [Tour](tour.qmd).

## The claims, precisely scoped

Every headline claim on this site states its scope and the command that
verifies it. These are the four that matter.

::: {.claim}
**Dual-implementation byte-identity.** The ~52K-line Rust reference and
the self-hosted Jestyr port emit byte-identical C over the 148-file
corpus, the concatenated self-hosting build, and the compiler's own
source. *Scope:* the single-file / concatenated emission path — the path
the corpus, the fixed point, and the seed all use. The module-loader
path has three known, documented divergences, pinned by their own test.
<span class="verify">$ cargo test --features c-oracle,selfhost-fixpoint</span>
:::

::: {.claim}
**The self-hosting fixed point.** The Jestyr-written compiler (29,818
lines of Jestyr, 162 `unsafe` mentions — 0.5% of lines), compiled by
itself, reproduces its own C output exactly: jc2 ≡ jc1. *Scope:*
verified on Windows and on Ubuntu CI; the gcc-only two-command demo
above is the same check without Rust.
<span class="verify">$ ./jc bootstrap/jestyr_flat.jtr > regen.c && diff regen.c bootstrap/jestyr_seed.c</span>
:::

::: {.claim}
**Cross-OS determinism.** A purified SHA-256 canary — integer ops plus
Jestyr's own float formatter, SIMD lane width included — produces the
digest `4389bf83…` identically on Windows 11 + MinGW gcc and Ubuntu
24.04 + gcc 13.3.0: two OSes, two libcs, one digest, re-checked by CI on
every push. `pi.jtr`: 20 consecutive runs, 20 identical outputs.
*Scope:* those two platforms; macOS/clang is untested.
<span class="verify">$ cargo test --features c-oracle determinism</span>
:::

::: {.claim}
**Speed parity with hand-written C.** Twin programs with byte-identical
output, medians: fib(40) 0.984×, numeric kernel ~1.0×, sieve 0.91×,
matmul 0.96×, wordcount 1.37× (Jestyr's strmap beats
`std::unordered_map`); honest loss on parallel sum at 0.60× (par-for
machinery vs hand-tuned threading — a named optimization target).
*Scope:* one machine (Windows 11, gcc/g++ 8.3, -O2, medians); correctness is
cross-platform via CI, timings are local. Full tables and methodology in
[Performance](performance.qmd).
<span class="verify">$ cargo test --features c-oracle cpp_compare</span>
:::

Behind these sit 916 green default tests, the full C-oracle ladder, and
a CI matrix (Ubuntu + Windows) that runs the corpus goldens, the
bootstrap job, and the determinism canary on every push.
